summary:
Still Here is a three-minute animated short film that brings NASA's abandoned machines back to life. Inspired by Toy Story, our characters Roo (the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle), Eagle (the Apollo 11 lunar module descent stage), Sojo (Sojourner) and Oppy (Opportunity) wake up when humans leave the Moon and Mars, and freeze whenever people appear. Created in a hand-painted, Studio Ghibli-inspired style with Gemini, the film follows Roo as he narrates each machine's story.

The project addresses the challenge directly. It introduces each piece of equipment, explains its original purpose, and shares the science it made possible: Apollo moon samples that revealed how the Moon formed, Sojourner proving rovers could work on Mars, and Opportunity finding evidence that liquid water once shaped the planet. It also explains why each was left behind, from the weight limits of lunar liftoff to lost contact and a global dust storm. All facts come from NASA's free, open mission data.

It matters because school-age learners usually hear only about active missions, while these machines paved the way for today's exploration. By turning dense technical history into friendship and emotion, Still Here makes space history memorable, honors past missions, and inspires the next generation of explorers. Abandoned, but not forgotten.
details:
What it does and how it works

Still Here is a three-minute animated short film that brings NASA's abandoned machines back to life. Inspired by Toy Story, Roo (the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle), Eagle (the Apollo 11 lunar module descent stage), Sojo (Sojourner) and Oppy (Opportunity) wake up when humans leave the Moon and Mars, and freeze whenever people appear. Roo narrates each machine's purpose, science mission, and why it was left behind.

Benefits and intended impact

Students learn real space history through friendship instead of dense technical websites. Teachers and parents get a ready-to-use story for introducing space exploration. The film shows that past missions paved the way for today's achievements, and inspires the next generation of explorers.

Tools and software

We used Gemini to generate character designs, backgrounds and video clips, with prompts written for a hand-painted, Studio Ghibli-inspired 2D style. We used an AI assistant to help draft prompts and scripts, CAPCUT for editing, and VOICEOVER TOOLS FROM CAPCUT for narration. No coding languages or hardware were used. Facts come from NASA's free, open data, including JPL's Sojourner mission pages, NASA's Opportunity mission reports, and Apollo archives.

Creativity

We turned dry mission history into an emotional story with a Toy Story-style rule: the machines come alive only when no one is watching. Each machine has its own personality, and the ending shows an astronaut saluting Roo, who secretly blinks back.

Factors we considered

Scientific accuracy, a young audience, consistent characters, and respect for the missions. We kept facts simple, checked dates and mission lengths against NASA sources, and used AI as a creative tool, not a replacement for the story.
